content: The evidence presented evaluates various methods of cervical preparation for surgical abortion, particularly focusing on the use of medications such as mifepristone and misoprostol, mechanical methods like osmotic dilators, and combinations of these approaches. 1. Cervical Dilation with Mifepristone and Misoprostol: Women who received mifepristone and misoprostol experienced greater cervical dilation before the procedure compared to those who received misoprostol alone. However, the certainty of this evidence is very low. When mifepristone was combined with sublingual misoprostol, cervical dilation was greater than with sublingual misoprostol alone. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. Conversely, when mifepristone was combined with vaginal misoprostol, cervical dilation was less than with vaginal misoprostol alone. The certainty of this evidence is low. 2. Need for Additional Dilation: Fewer women in the mifepristone and misoprostol group required further cervical dilation compared to those in the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. 3. Procedure Completion Time: The time required to complete the procedure was shorter with mifepristone and misoprostol compared to misoprostol alone. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. Specifically, the combination of mifepristone and sublingual misoprostol resulted in shorter procedure times compared to sublingual misoprostol alone. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. Similarly, the combination of mifepristone and vaginal misoprostol resulted in shorter procedure times compared to vaginal misoprostol alone. The certainty of this evidence is low. 4. Provider Satisfaction: Providers expressed greater satisfaction with the use of mifepristone and misoprostol compared to misoprostol alone for cervical priming prior to surgical abortion. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. 5. Cervical Tears: Fewer women in the mifepristone and misoprostol group experienced cervical tears compared to those in the misoprostol-only group. However, the certainty of this evidence is very low. 6. Undesirable Effects: Women in the mifepristone and misoprostol group reported lower satisfaction rates compared to those in the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of this evidence is low. More women in the mifepristone and misoprostol group experienced side effects such as nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea compared to the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of this evidence ranges from low to moderate. Pre-procedure expulsion of the pregnancy occurred more frequently in the mifepristone and misoprostol group compared to the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. 7. Comparison of Medical and Mechanical Methods: Procedures completed with medical methods (e.g., misoprostol) were faster than those completed with mechanical methods (e.g., osmotic dilators). The certainty of this evidence is very low. Fewer women in the medical methods group experienced nausea compared to those in the mechanical methods group. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. Fewer women in the medical methods group experienced bleeding compared to those in the mechanical methods group. The certainty of this evidence is low. Fewer women in the medical methods group required additional interventions compared to those in the mechanical methods group. The certainty of this evidence is low. There were no differences between the groups in terms of uterine perforation rates. The certainty of this evidence is low. Fewer women in the medical methods group reported post-procedure pain compared to those in the mechanical methods group. The certainty of this evidence is very low. 8. Pre-Procedure Cervical Dilation: Women in the medical methods group had less cervical dilation before the procedure compared to those in the mechanical methods group. The certainty of this evidence is low. Specifically, women who received mifepristone alone had less cervical dilation compared to those who underwent mechanical methods. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. Women who received misoprostol alone also had less cervical dilation compared to those who underwent mechanical methods. The certainty of this evidence is low. 9. Ease of Procedure: The ease of performing the procedure was noted to be lower in the medical methods group compared to the mechanical methods group. 10. Recommendations for Cervical Priming: For surgical abortion at 12–19 weeks of gestation, cervical priming with medication alone (preferably a combination of mifepristone and misoprostol) or a combination of medication and osmotic dilators is suggested. When using osmotic dilators, the interval between placement and the procedure should not exceed two days. For surgical abortion at ≥19 weeks, cervical priming with both osmotic dilators and medication (mifepristone, misoprostol, or both) is recommended. 11. Research Evidence: The evidence base for these recommendations includes 16 studies from various countries, evaluating both medical and mechanical methods of cervical preparation. The studies assessed desirable and undesirable effects, certainty of evidence, values, and the balance of effects. This detailed analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of the relative benefits and drawbacks of different cervical preparation methods for surgical abortion, with varying levels of evidence certainty.
